# Porting an xscreensaver hack

The rules live in `AGENTS.md` ("Rules", "Gotchas") and the path-scoped notes in
`.claude/rules/`. This skill sets the order of work and the points to stop. The
numbered steps are in `adding-a-hack.md` and the recipes it names are in
`techniques.md`, both next to this file. For several hacks in one go, read
`batches.md` too.

## 1. Pick, then read the source

Take S-rated rows from `docs/porting-assessment.md` first, and prefer a low
**Speed** band: the table runs each unported S hack on the host. The effort
rating counts missing shim calls, not memory, speed or stack (Braid was S, and
would have shown as high). A high band is a hack that will probably run slowly
on the board; a low band is not a guarantee, because a hack still doing
software `double` maths runs far slower on the device than on the host. Read
the hack's source before copying it, and look for:

| The source has | Technique (seen in) |
| --- | --- |
| Arrays or a state over a few MB | Build-time patch (Maze) |
| `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt`, `pow`, `double` in a hot loop | Single precision (Galaxy, Substrate) |
| Locals over a few KB | Stack check (Rorschach) |
| An allocation of 100 KB or more, or `exit()` on failure | Large allocations (Substrate) |
| Pixmaps, clip masks, a logo image | Images (Maze) |
| A hack that restarts itself | Restart leak test (Maze, Substrate) |
| A `free` that relies on state `draw` sets up (a lazy `initted`) | Stopping before the first draw (Blaster) |
| Hairlines, fades or `glPolygonOffset` in a GL hack | Thin lines in a GL hack |
| Threads, GL, Xft, shared memory | Skipping a hack |
| A licence header | Read it; add a notices section only if it differs from jwz's |

## 2. Set up

Work in a worktree off `origin/main`. Its setup and the commands it refuses are
in "Worktree setup".

## 3. Red, copy, green

Follow `adding-a-hack.md`. Show the registry test failing before
copying. Fill each shim gap test-first, then break the code on purpose and
watch the test fail ("Tests that cannot be fooled"). Filling a missing
function is a shim gap. Changing what every hack sees (the runner, a default, a
shared helper) is not: stop and ask Rod first. A speed-up in the shared GL
layer counts too, even when every pinned frame hash still matches (HexTrail's
deferred depth clear): ask before writing it, and name it in the PR body.

## 4. Verify on the host

Run `pio test -e native`, `uv run --with pytest --with pillow pytest tools/tests`
and `uv run tools/check_notices.py`, and dump frames at several counts. Host
frames cannot show a byte swap, which happens in the push to the display: judge
colour on the device, on a colour you know the answer to.

## 5. Device

Flash only after Rod says so in this conversation; approval for one flash is
not approval for the next. See "Device capture". Report "compiles", "host tests
pass" and "runs on the device" separately; only Rod can say what the screen
shows. If it is slow, measure, change one thing, flash again and compare; if it
is still slow, say so and suggest dropping it. A hack that runs at a good rate
can still go: Rod dropped Boing (8.3 fps, "pretty boring on a small screen")
and asked for HexTrail to be tuned because it fell under 10 fps before the
rotation moved on. Judge a hack on a 466 px round screen, and by its worst
window as well as its mean. Record the numbers in
`tools/assessment_measured.md`, marking anything unmeasured as such.

## 6. Deliver

Commit named paths. Open the draft PR with `entire trail create` and put what
is unverified in its body. After a rebase, a push needs `--force-with-lease`:
ask Rod each time. Rod approves and merges; then delete the branch and
fast-forward `main`. New gotchas go in the matching `.claude/rules/` file (or
`AGENTS.md` if they apply everywhere) in the same PR, and deferred
ideas become issues.

## Red flags

| Thought | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| "It is rated S, so I need not read it" | Maze was rated L for Xlib gaps; the real blocker was a 20 MB `calloc`. |
| "It compiles, so it works" | Rorschach compiled and rebooted on its first frame. |
| "The colours look right" | Not from a host frame: every hack was byte swapped until Maze. |
| "My test passes, so it tests something" | A test through Pyro passed with the runner broken. Break the code on purpose. |
| "AGENTS.md says to fix shim gaps, so I can change the runner" | A new function is a gap. A change every hack sees needs Rod. |
| "Rod approved flashing earlier" | Ask again for each flash. |
| "Single precision is done, so the hack is as fast as it gets" | HexTrail gained 0.3 fps from it and 2.3 from a depth clear in the GL layer. Read what the shared code does each frame. |
| "The mean is above 10 fps" | HexTrail's mean was 15.3 and its worst window 10.8; its step grew all cycle. Read the lowest window. |

# Porting a batch of hacks

For several hacks on one branch, with Rod away. The per-hack steps are in
`SKILL.md` and `adding-a-hack.md`; this is what a batch adds. Per-hack findings
live in `.claude/rules/hacks.md`, not here.

## Order of work

1. Read every header before copying anything: a `(GPL)` tag or an xlock notice
   changes the notices row, and a licence that is not a permission notice means
   stop and ask.
2. Triage by gap count. Do the easy ones first: they pay for shim gaps the
   others need. Leave GL and anything under a few fps to last.
3. One branch, a commit per hack, shim code test-first and mutation-checked.
   No PR until Rod says.
4. `uv run tools/wire_hack.py <name> <Class> "<copyright>"` copies the file and
   registers it with a frame hash of `0` (skipped), so every commit stays green.
   Then `pio run -e dump`, fill the gaps, dump frames at several counts and
   look at them.
5. Flash and measure each hack as soon as it runs
   (`bash tools/flash_and_capture.sh <hack> 30`). Report measured, unjudged and
   unseen separately.
6. Pin all the new hashes in one run, after looking at the frames:
   `HACK_PINS_OUT=<file> pio test -e native -f test_hacks`.
7. Soak the whole registry before handing over: `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5` for five
   laps, then look for a reboot, a panic or a "Stack canary", and compare PSRAM
   on each visit of the new hacks (it should match exactly).
8. Measured rows, rules, a regenerated assessment, and a notes file for Rod: what
   to look at, which choices are his, what was not measured. His review changes
   the numbers (a hack dropped, one retuned), so rewrite the notes after it or
   put the final state in the PR body, which is the record. A stale notes file
   misleads.

## Traps

| Trap | Do |
| --- | --- |
| A change that is not pixel-identical by construction (single precision, a faster fill) and you only checked fps | Look at a frame. A hack drew garbage for hours at "20 fps" |
| `#define double float` before a header that has `double` in a struct a shim `.c` shares | Include that header first, then the define; a flat-screen test guards it |
| A hack that keeps state in statics across starts | Its pin depends on earlier tests; reset the static in a wrapper, and test both outcomes |
| A mode picked with `random()` | A boot is deterministic, so measure the other mode by forcing it |
| Constants in pixels or frames, tuned for another window size or frame rate | Scale them at build time (`tools/fireworkx_patch.py`), not by editing the copy |
| A hack that treats `malloc(0) == NULL` as out of memory | The board returns NULL for zero bytes, the host a pointer: it stops drawing on the board only. Reproduce with an allocator hook that fails for zero |
| A stop that leaks | `MallocStackLogging=1 leaks --atExit -- .pio/build/dump/program <index> 0 out.raw` names the line (rebuild `-e dump` first) |

## Finding the cost

Skip one thing behind a temporary flag and read `step=`; revert it. Guessing
was wrong three times running. The usual causes here:

- full-frame passes over PSRAM: a clear, a copy, a blur, a 565 conversion (render
  smaller, alias a pixmap to the window, erase only what was drawn)
- the shim's polygon fill, which divides in double (`hacks/float_polygon.h`)
- soft double: `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm <object> | grep ' U __.*df'`; `frand` hides
  a `1.0` in its macro body (`hacks/single_frand.h`)
- a pause the hack asks for (`wait=`): override `*delay` and say the pace changed
- a GL hack's clear and push, which scale with the dirty box, and work the GL
  layer does that nothing reads (a depth clear with the depth test off):
  `gl_budget.py` shows vertices submitted against triangles drawn

## Choices for Rod

When look and speed trade off, leave a build flag per option, measure each, and
register the one nearer his bar. After his hands-on notes, expect to retune or
drop: from seven ports he kept six and dropped Boing, and asked for HexTrail to
be faster. Keep a flashable rotation build ready (`-DROTATE_SECONDS=25`, the new
hacks first) and say which build the board holds when you stop.

## Tools

| Register a hack | `tools/wire_hack.py` |
| Flash a pinned build and read the serial log | `tools/flash_and_capture.sh`, `tools/serial_capture.py` |
| Does a test notice a break | `tools/mutate.py <file> 'old=>new' --cmd '...'` |

# Adding a hack

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md. The order of work is in `SKILL.md`.

The `port-hack` skill orders this work, says what to read for before copying a
hack, and holds a recipe per trap. The steps:

1. Check its row in `docs/porting-assessment.md` (effort and Speed band) and
   read its licence header.
2. Update the expected list in `firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c` and see
   it fail.
3. Copy the file to `firmware/src/hacks/<name>/<name>.c`, add the notices row
   and an `extern` plus entry in `hacks/registry.c`.
4. Fill shim gaps test-first in `firmware/test/test_xshim/`. The compile
   check in `score_hacks.py` shows what is missing.
5. Host tests pass, dump a frame and look at it, then (with Rod's go-ahead)
   flash and measure fps and free heap/PSRAM over serial. To pin its frame
   hash after looking at the frame, put `0x1ull` in `kBaseline`, run
   `pio test -e native -f test_hacks`, convert the "Was N" in the failure line
   with `python3 -c "print(hex(N))"`, and run it again.
6. Regenerate the assessment and add measurements to
   `tools/assessment_measured.md`, then re-run the speed backtest: each port
   adds a point to the check of the Speed bands, which were fitted to the first
   29 hacks. To make a port a real test, commit its host time and predicted
   range first (`docs/speed-predictions.md` shows the form), flash it as copied,
   and add its name to `HOLDOUT` in `tools/speed_backtest.py`. The first four
   (Mountain, Epicycle, Kaleidescope, Celtic) all fell where predicted.
7. If a hack is slow and `double`-heavy (many `double`s, `sqrt`, `sin`/`cos`,
   `pow`), try a single-precision wrapper like `hacks/galaxy_single.c` (for a
   plain screenhack, `hacks/substrate_single.c`; the recipe is in the skill's
   `techniques.md`), and compare double and float frames at several frame
   counts. A resource
   override can skip a hack's restart cleanup: Galaxy leaked at `count: 2`, so
   leak-test any override.
8. If Rod drops a port after seeing it (Hypnowheel, Boing; Celtic was dropped
   and came back through issue #37): remove it
   from `g_hacks[]`, the expected list, its hash and its leak test; keep the
   source and notices row; add `name: reason` (short: it is printed as a
   bullet) to `tools/failed_ports.txt`. For a GL hack, keep the `<name>_gl.c`
   wrapper but exclude it and the directory (`-<hacks/boing/>
   -<hacks/boing_gl.c>`) in all three `build_src_filter` lines, or it still
   builds. A reason Rod gave in his own words ("boring on a small screen") is
   the reason to record. File an issue only if there is something to come back
   to.
# Porting techniques

Recipes for the traps listed in `SKILL.md`. Each says when it applies, what to
do, and what it did the last time.

## Build-time patch

When: the hack's own constants make it too big for the board. Maze keeps a
1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one `calloc`, about
20 MB, and the board has 8 MB of PSRAM.

- The copy in `hacks/<name>/` stays byte-identical to upstream (`cmp` it).
- A PlatformIO `pre:` script (`firmware/patch_maze.py`) writes a patched copy
  into the build directory, using a tested function (`tools/maze_patch.py`)
  that raises if upstream's lines change. A wrapper (`hacks/maze_small.c`)
  includes that copy, and the original is excluded in `build_src_filter` of
  all three environments (`stopwatch`, `native`, `dump`).
- Maze's limits went from 1000 to 80: about 125 KB.
- A patch can switch off a branch (Pacman's `NRAND (2) == 0` becomes `0`) or
  replace a whole function (its route search becomes a loop). Check the
  original's SHA-256 so an upstream edit fails the build. Before a rewrite, pin
  a long-run fingerprint taken with the original (30,000 frames, every ghost's
  position every 100), show the code ran, and mutate the order to watch the pin
  fail.

## Single precision

When: a hot loop does `double` maths or calls `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt` or `pow`.
The ESP32-S3 has a single-precision FPU only, so double runs in software.

- Find the hot loop first and count the calls. Substrate makes four `sin` calls
  per sand grain, with 64 grains a crack and up to 100 cracks: about 25,000
  software `sin`s a frame. Its step grew from 5 ms to 121 ms as the picture
  filled.
- Wrapper `hacks/<name>_single.c`: include the framework headers first, then
  `hacks/single_precision.h`, then the unmodified hack. Exclude the original in
  `build_src_filter` of all three environments.
- `M_PI` is a double literal, so the angle arithmetic stays double: put
  `#undef M_PI` and a float definition after the header. Literals such as
  `0.81` stay double too, and a header cannot change them: `0.5 * x` with a
  float `x` is software double maths. Check the wrapper's object for soft-double
  helpers with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm braid.o | grep ' U __.*df'` (compile with
  `-Os -mlongcalls` and the shim's include paths). If any remain, rewrite the
  literals at build time as Braid does: `tools/float_literals.py` (tested, skips
  strings and comments) run by `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`, and the
  wrapper includes `<name>_floatlit.c` from the build directory. GCC's
  `-fsingle-precision-constant` does the same, but Apple clang ignores it, so
  host tests would run other arithmetic than the board.
- Galaxy, Drift, Discrete, Flame and Substrate were wrapped before this check
  and have not been looked at for double literals.
- Hand-written `sin` and `cos` (`hacks/fast_trig.h`) moved Braid by 5%. Do the
  literals first.
- Compare double and float frames at several counts. Early frames match; a
  chaotic hack diverges later but should keep its look.
- GL hacks too: Hypnowheel's spiral called `cos` and `sin` in `double` for
  every vertex, about 275 ms of a 706 ms step, hidden behind a fill-heavy look.
  Its wrapper (`hypnowheel_single_gl.c`) adapts `get_position` and
  `get_rotation` as HexTrail's does.
- Results: Galaxy 5 to 14 fps. Substrate step 119-121 ms to 37-38 ms, 6.2 to
  12.5 fps.
- A hack that passes the address of its own `double` local to a shim function
  (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &s, &v)`) writes eight bytes into a four-byte float, and
  the compiler does not warn. Moire's frames were all different from the
  double build's until `moire_single.c` mapped the call to an adapter defined
  before `single_precision.h`. Cmp the wrapper's frames against the unmodified
  hack's. A hack with no decimal literals must stay out of
  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses it.
- Once the maths is float, look at the fills before the next idea. CWaves'
  cosines were 4 ms of a 61 ms step; its 233 column fills were 57 (a thin
  full-height rectangle touches a new cache line a store). See `hacks.md`.
- A float build can break a check that held in double. Both the S3 (`madd.s`)
  and arm64 fuse a multiply and an add, so `t*n - floor(t*n)` uses the exact
  product for the subtraction and the rounded one for the `floor`, and can
  come out slightly negative: Celtic's `assert(tt>=0 && tt<1)` aborted at
  t 0.331093 with 3422 segments. The 3000-frame test (`pio test`) found it
  on the host, and the same abort would have hit the board. Compute the
  product once in a build-time patch (`tools/celtic_patch.py`). Map any libm
  call the hack makes that `single_precision.h` does not (`rint`, `floor`),
  and check the object with `nm` for `__*df*` helpers, not only `__muldf3`.

## Slow hack

When: a ported hack runs under about 10 fps and the push is not the cause
(`step` in the serial line is large).

- For a GL hack, flash a `-DGL_PROFILE` build first (AGENTS.md): it splits
  the frame into stages, and time in none of them is the hack's own code.
  Issue #73 guessed Hypnowheel was 70 percent blended fill; the profile showed
  a third of its frame was `double` trig.
- A worst-case microbenchmark is not the workload. A PSRAM cache miss costs
  about 220 cycles, which suggested GL fill was memory-bound; a banded renderer
  in internal RAM, built on that, was exact and slower (neighbouring triangles
  share cache lines). A/B the first working slice of a speed idea on the board
  before building the rest, and stop if it does not pay.
- Do not trust a host profile (`sample` on the dump program) for where the
  time goes. A Mac does `double` at full speed, so software-double code looks
  cheap there: Braid's disc fill was 6% on the host and the largest cost on the
  board.
- Split the step on the device with a temporary build flag that makes the
  expensive call return at once (Braid: `XDrawLine`). The step left is the
  hack's own cost; the difference is the drawing. Remove the flag before
  committing.
- Count what is called per frame (segments, calls, rows) before guessing,
  and look at the object file for soft-double helpers (see "Single precision").
- Change one thing, pin that the pixels did not move (`cmp` frames at several
  counts, or the pinned hash), flash, and compare second windows. Braid's four
  changes were worth 2.7-3.2 times, 1.05, and 1.3.
- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1) are the costly path: a quad filled a row at
  a time, plus two discs for round caps. `stroke.c` keeps a table of disc rows
  by width up to 16. A wide full circle through `XDrawArc` is about a thousand
  such segments (Deluxe: 94% of a frame, 2-5 fps); `stroke_circle` fills it as
  a ring in two spans a row.
- When the cost is overpaint, not `double` maths, a host split does find the
  dominant call: `#define XDrawArc(...) 0` in the wrapper, `pio run -e dump`,
  then `/usr/bin/time -p .pio/build/dump/program <index> 400 out.raw` three
  times, against the baseline. It cannot see costs that live in memory
  traffic (Deluxe's alpha mask: nothing on the host, 3-5 ms on the board).
- Counting works where timing misleads: a scratch copy of the hack with a
  counter in the inner function and a macro round `XDrawLine` gave Celtic's
  spline evaluations and line draws per draw call on the host, by graph type.
  A cost per eval and per line fitted to a first device capture (about 1.7 us
  and 22 us, from three graph types and a handful of windows) estimated 63 ms
  for the biggest type after the change; the next capture's 12.6-76.8 ms did
  not contradict it, but the log does not say which type each window was, so
  the fit is unchecked.
- A hack's own pacing constants can be the lever: Celtic's 0.0001 tick (a
  patch scales it, `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE`) set both the look-ahead's work and how
  many draw calls a picture takes. Count the draw calls a picture takes and
  the pause after it before reading `fps=`: with a 5 s pause the column read
  5.2 in every window and measured the pause, not the drawing. Use
  `1000 / (step + push + delay)` for the drawing rate.
- Heap and speed were two problems in Celtic and one fix cured only the
  first: the graph sized to the screen cut a pattern's heap about 9 times and
  left spline evaluations per call unchanged. Measure both after each change.
- A hack that redraws its whole picture every frame to animate colour (Braid)
  costs its full draw each frame whatever the push does. Check this before
  porting; the scorer does not flag it yet.
- A fix that moves the frame rate by under 5% shows the maths was not the
  cost. HexTrail in single precision went from 12.7 to 13.0 fps; the 2.3 fps
  that mattered came from reading what the GL layer does each frame
  (`glshim_clear`) and finding a depth clear that nothing read, because the hack
  never enables the depth test. Run `nm` on the object, then read the shared
  code the hack calls before trying a third idea in the hack.
- A step that grows over the hack's cycle (HexTrail: 19 ms to a ceiling, then it
  restarts) needs the worst window, not the mean. Capture at least one full
  cycle (150 s covered HexTrail's 65 s), read the lowest `fps=`, and compare the
  time spent below 10 fps with the rotation interval: Rod saw it fall under 10
  before the 25 s change. If a resource such as `count` scales the cost, give it
  an `#ifndef` default in `registry.c` (`HEXTRAIL_COUNT`) so one flash tests
  another value, and measure two or three values: count 6 gave a mean of 12.7,
  10 gave 9.1 and 20 gave 5.7, in double precision.

## Thin lines in a GL hack

When: a GL hack draws hairlines or fades (Unknown Pleasures) and looks right
in a host frame but flickers on the board. Work down this list, one layer at a
time, and look at the screen (or film) after each; each layer hid the next.

- Lines hop. TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel, so a drifting line
  jumps. `tinygl_patch.py` keeps the fractional position and draws a Wu line
  when the hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Triangles are still snapped.
- Quads that hide the lines behind them hide nothing, or the picture is
  speckled grey. TinyGL's blend adds colours, ignores alpha and misreads our
  byte-swapped pixels, so `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA` is drawn as an
  opaque fill. Smooth lines carry no alpha, so a hack's per-line fade is lost.
- A line drawn on its own polygon's edge is erased in dashes: `glPolygonOffset`
  was stored and never read. The patch applies it, plus a margin for the
  vertex snapping. Check the effect on the host by the second difference of a
  frame's total brightness while the picture drifts a fraction of a pixel; change
  one thing at a time, because blending once made the experiment unable to
  show any effect.
- Pieces of a line vanish for one refresh. The panel scans while the push
  writes, so a seam crosses the picture. Set `sync_to_refresh` on the hack
  (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`); see `.claude/rules/device-display.md` for the
  offset, why it is only valid for a full-frame push, and how to film the
  result. Cost: up to a refresh of latency a frame, so only a hack that needs
  it should ask.
- Budget with `gl_budget.py` but expect it to be off: it has no blend term
  (Unknown Pleasures was predicted at 251 ms and ran at 267, then 197 once the
  fills were opaque). Add the measured row as a calibration point.
- After all that a dimming of about 14% for 25 ms at each push remained (issue
  #68). Do not promise a hack is flicker-free from a host frame or from the
  absence of vanishing lines alone.

## Stack check

When: locals over a few KB. Compile the hack with `-O1 -fstack-usage` (flags in
AGENTS.md) and keep each frame well under the 16 KB loop stack. Host tests
cannot see an overflow: Rorschach's 9.6 KB array rebooted the device on its

Recursion: replay it, don't guess. Run the hack on a pthread with a painted
1 MB stack over several seeds and thousands of frames (Pacman's generator: 236

decode a panic backtrace with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-addr2line` against an ELF

45	# Porting techniques
46	
47	Recipes for the traps listed in `SKILL.md`. Each says when it applies, what to
48	do, and what it did the last time.
49	
50	## Build-time patch
51	
52	When: the hack's own constants make it too big for the board. Maze keeps a
53	1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one `calloc`, about
54	20 MB, and the board has 8 MB of PSRAM.
55	
56	- The copy in `hacks/<name>/` stays byte-identical to upstream (`cmp` it).
57	- A PlatformIO `pre:` script (`firmware/patch_maze.py`) writes a patched copy
58	  into the build directory, using a tested function (`tools/maze_patch.py`)
59	  that raises if upstream's lines change. A wrapper (`hacks/maze_small.c`)
60	  includes that copy, and the original is excluded in `build_src_filter` of
61	  all three environments (`stopwatch`, `native`, `dump`).
62	- Maze's limits went from 1000 to 80: about 125 KB.
63	- A patch can switch off a branch (Pacman's `NRAND (2) == 0` becomes `0`) or
64	  replace a whole function (its route search becomes a loop). Check the
65	  original's SHA-256 so an upstream edit fails the build. Before a rewrite, pin
66	  a long-run fingerprint taken with the original (30,000 frames, every ghost's
67	  position every 100), show the code ran, and mutate the order to watch the pin
68	  fail.
69	
70	## Single precision
71	
72	When: a hot loop does `double` maths or calls `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt` or `pow`.
73	The ESP32-S3 has a single-precision FPU only, so double runs in software.
74	
75	- Find the hot loop first and count the calls. Substrate makes four `sin` calls
76	  per sand grain, with 64 grains a crack and up to 100 cracks: about 25,000
77	  software `sin`s a frame. Its step grew from 5 ms to 121 ms as the picture
78	  filled.
79	- Wrapper `hacks/<name>_single.c`: include the framework headers first, then
80	  `hacks/single_precision.h`, then the unmodified hack. Exclude the original in
81	  `build_src_filter` of all three environments.
82	- `M_PI` is a double literal, so the angle arithmetic stays double: put
83	  `#undef M_PI` and a float definition after the header. Literals such as
84	  `0.81` stay double too, and a header cannot change them: `0.5 * x` with a
85	  float `x` is software double maths. Check the wrapper's object for soft-double
86	  helpers with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm braid.o | grep ' U __.*df'` (compile with
87	  `-Os -mlongcalls` and the shim's include paths). If any remain, rewrite the
88	  literals at build time as Braid does: `tools/float_literals.py` (tested, skips
89	  strings and comments) run by `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`, and the
90	  wrapper includes `<name>_floatlit.c` from the build directory. GCC's
91	  `-fsingle-precision-constant` does the same, but Apple clang ignores it, so
92	  host tests would run other arithmetic than the board.
93	- Galaxy, Drift, Discrete, Flame and Substrate were wrapped before this check
94	  and have not been looked at for double literals.
95	- Hand-written `sin` and `cos` (`hacks/fast_trig.h`) moved Braid by 5%. Do the
96	  literals first.
97	- Compare double and float frames at several counts. Early frames match; a
98	  chaotic hack diverges later but should keep its look.
99	- GL hacks too: Hypnowheel's spiral called `cos` and `sin` in `double` for
100	  every vertex, about 275 ms of a 706 ms step, hidden behind a fill-heavy look.
101	  Its wrapper (`hypnowheel_single_gl.c`) adapts `get_position` and
102	  `get_rotation` as HexTrail's does.
103	- Results: Galaxy 5 to 14 fps. Substrate step 119-121 ms to 37-38 ms, 6.2 to
104	  12.5 fps.
105	- A hack that passes the address of its own `double` local to a shim function
106	  (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &s, &v)`) writes eight bytes into a four-byte float, and
107	  the compiler does not warn. Moire's frames were all different from the
108	  double build's until `moire_single.c` mapped the call to an adapter defined
109	  before `single_precision.h`. Cmp the wrapper's frames against the unmodified
110	  hack's. A hack with no decimal literals must stay out of
111	  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses it.
112	- Once the maths is float, look at the fills before the next idea. CWaves'
113	  cosines were 4 ms of a 61 ms step; its 233 column fills were 57 (a thin
114	  full-height rectangle touches a new cache line a store). See `hacks.md`.
115	- A float build can break a check that held in double. Both the S3 (`madd.s`)
116	  and arm64 fuse a multiply and an add, so `t*n - floor(t*n)` uses the exact
117	  product for the subtraction and the rounded one for the `floor`, and can
118	  come out slightly negative: Celtic's `assert(tt>=0 && tt<1)` aborted at
119	  t 0.331093 with 3422 segments. The 3000-frame test (`pio test`) found it
120	  on the host, and the same abort would have hit the board. Compute the
121	  product once in a build-time patch (`tools/celtic_patch.py`). Map any libm
122	  call the hack makes that `single_precision.h` does not (`rint`, `floor`),
123	  and check the object with `nm` for `__*df*` helpers, not only `__muldf3`.
124	
125	## Slow hack
126	
127	When: a ported hack runs under about 10 fps and the push is not the cause
128	(`step` in the serial line is large).
129	
130	- For a GL hack, flash a `-DGL_PROFILE` build first (AGENTS.md): it splits
131	  the frame into stages, and time in none of them is the hack's own code.
132	  Issue #73 guessed Hypnowheel was 70 percent blended fill; the profile showed
133	  a third of its frame was `double` trig.
134	- A worst-case microbenchmark is not the workload. A PSRAM cache miss costs
135	  about 220 cycles, which suggested GL fill was memory-bound; a banded renderer
136	  in internal RAM, built on that, was exact and slower (neighbouring triangles
137	  share cache lines). A/B the first working slice of a speed idea on the board
138	  before building the rest, and stop if it does not pay.
139	- Do not trust a host profile (`sample` on the dump program) for where the
140	  time goes. A Mac does `double` at full speed, so software-double code looks
141	  cheap there: Braid's disc fill was 6% on the host and the largest cost on the
142	  board.
143	- Split the step on the device with a temporary build flag that makes the
144	  expensive call return at once (Braid: `XDrawLine`). The step left is the
145	  hack's own cost; the difference is the drawing. Remove the flag before
146	  committing.
147	- Count what is called per frame (segments, calls, rows) before guessing,
148	  and look at the object file for soft-double helpers (see "Single precision").
149	- Change one thing, pin that the pixels did not move (`cmp` frames at several
150	  counts, or the pinned hash), flash, and compare second windows. Braid's four
151	  changes were worth 2.7-3.2 times, 1.05, and 1.3.
152	- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1) are the costly path: a quad filled a row at
153	  a time, plus two discs for round caps. `stroke.c` keeps a table of disc rows
154	  by width up to 16. A wide full circle through `XDrawArc` is about a thousand
155	  such segments (Deluxe: 94% of a frame, 2-5 fps); `stroke_circle` fills it as
156	  a ring in two spans a row.
157	- When the cost is overpaint, not `double` maths, a host split does find the
158	  dominant call: `#define XDrawArc(...) 0` in the wrapper, `pio run -e dump`,
159	  then `/usr/bin/time -p .pio/build/dump/program <index> 400 out.raw` three
160	  times, against the baseline. It cannot see costs that live in memory
161	  traffic (Deluxe's alpha mask: nothing on the host, 3-5 ms on the board).
162	- Counting works where timing misleads: a scratch copy of the hack with a
163	  counter in the inner function and a macro round `XDrawLine` gave Celtic's
164	  spline evaluations and line draws per draw call on the host, by graph type.
165	  A cost per eval and per line fitted to a first device capture (about 1.7 us
166	  and 22 us, from three graph types and a handful of windows) estimated 63 ms
167	  for the biggest type after the change; the next capture's 12.6-76.8 ms did
168	  not contradict it, but the log does not say which type each window was, so
169	  the fit is unchecked.
170	- A hack's own pacing constants can be the lever: Celtic's 0.0001 tick (a
171	  patch scales it, `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE`) set both the look-ahead's work and how
172	  many draw calls a picture takes. Count the draw calls a picture takes and
173	  the pause after it before reading `fps=`: with a 5 s pause the column read
174	  5.2 in every window and measured the pause, not the drawing. Use
175	  `1000 / (step + push + delay)` for the drawing rate.
176	- Heap and speed were two problems in Celtic and one fix cured only the
177	  first: the graph sized to the screen cut a pattern's heap about 9 times and
178	  left spline evaluations per call unchanged. Measure both after each change.
179	- A hack that redraws its whole picture every frame to animate colour (Braid)
180	  costs its full draw each frame whatever the push does. Check this before
181	  porting; the scorer does not flag it yet.
182	- A fix that moves the frame rate by under 5% shows the maths was not the
183	  cost. HexTrail in single precision went from 12.7 to 13.0 fps; the 2.3 fps
184	  that mattered came from reading what the GL layer does each frame
185	  (`glshim_clear`) and finding a depth clear that nothing read, because the hack
186	  never enables the depth test. Run `nm` on the object, then read the shared
187	  code the hack calls before trying a third idea in the hack.
188	- A step that grows over the hack's cycle (HexTrail: 19 ms to a ceiling, then it
189	  restarts) needs the worst window, not the mean. Capture at least one full
190	  cycle (150 s covered HexTrail's 65 s), read the lowest `fps=`, and compare the
191	  time spent below 10 fps with the rotation interval: Rod saw it fall under 10
192	  before the 25 s change. If a resource such as `count` scales the cost, give it
193	  an `#ifndef` default in `registry.c` (`HEXTRAIL_COUNT`) so one flash tests
194	  another value, and measure two or three values: count 6 gave a mean of 12.7,
195	  10 gave 9.1 and 20 gave 5.7, in double precision.
196	
197	## Thin lines in a GL hack
198	
199	When: a GL hack draws hairlines or fades (Unknown Pleasures) and looks right
200	in a host frame but flickers on the board. Work down this list, one layer at a
201	time, and look at the screen (or film) after each; each layer hid the next.
202	
203	- Lines hop. TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel, so a drifting line
204	  jumps. `tinygl_patch.py` keeps the fractional position and draws a Wu line
205	  when the hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Triangles are still snapped.
206	- Quads that hide the lines behind them hide nothing, or the picture is
207	  speckled grey. TinyGL's blend adds colours, ignores alpha and misreads our
208	  byte-swapped pixels, so `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA` is drawn as an
209	  opaque fill. Smooth lines carry no alpha, so a hack's per-line fade is lost.
210	- A line drawn on its own polygon's edge is erased in dashes: `glPolygonOffset`
211	  was stored and never read. The patch applies it, plus a margin for the
212	  vertex snapping. Check the effect on the host by the second difference of a
213	  frame's total brightness while the picture drifts a fraction of a pixel; change
214	  one thing at a time, because blending once made the experiment unable to
215	  show any effect.
216	- Pieces of a line vanish for one refresh. The panel scans while the push
217	  writes, so a seam crosses the picture. Set `sync_to_refresh` on the hack
218	  (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`); see `.claude/rules/device-display.md` for the
219	  offset, why it is only valid for a full-frame push, and how to film the
220	  result. Cost: up to a refresh of latency a frame, so only a hack that needs
221	  it should ask.
222	- Budget with `gl_budget.py` but expect it to be off: it has no blend term
223	  (Unknown Pleasures was predicted at 251 ms and ran at 267, then 197 once the
224	  fills were opaque). Add the measured row as a calibration point.
225	- After all that a dimming of about 14% for 25 ms at each push remained (issue
226	  #68). Do not promise a hack is flicker-free from a host frame or from the
227	  absence of vanishing lines alone.
228	
229	## Stack check
230	
231	When: locals over a few KB. Compile the hack with `-O1 -fstack-usage` (flags in
232	AGENTS.md) and keep each frame well under the 16 KB loop stack. Host tests
233	cannot see an overflow: Rorschach's 9.6 KB array rebooted the device on its
234	first frame, and only the serial log's "Stack canary" showed it.
235	
236	Recursion: replay it, don't guess. Run the hack on a pthread with a painted
237	1 MB stack over several seeds and thousands of frames (Pacman's generator: 236
238	KB median, 315 KB worst; `ulimit -s` saw only the first, shallow level). Read a
239	frame's size from the ELF (`xtensa-esp32s3-elf-objdump -d`, `entry a1, N`), and
240	decode a panic backtrace with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-addr2line` against an ELF
241	rebuilt with the same flags. A recursion over a grid is bounded by its cells:
242	replay it from every start.
243	
244	## Large allocations
245	
246	When: one allocation of 100 KB or more, or the hack calls `exit()` if it fails.
247	
248	- `unsigned long` is 4 bytes on the device and 8 on the host, so host leak
249	  numbers are double the device's.
250	- Plain `malloc` and `realloc` of two 868 KB buffers (Substrate) landed in
251	  PSRAM: free PSRAM fell by 1,742,096 bytes, which is 2 x 466 x 466 x 4 plus a
252	  few KB. Internal heap barely moved.
253	- On restart the buffers were freed and allocated again, and free PSRAM
254	  returned to the same value. Read heap and PSRAM in the log to confirm this
255	  for each large hack.
256	
257	## Images
258	
259	Colour pixmaps are canvases: every drawing primitive, `XCopyArea` and
260	`XCopyPlane` draw into them. Bitmaps take only `XCopyArea` from another
261	bitmap. There is no PNG
262	decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads a raw RGB565 blob and
263	mask (format in `ximage-loader.h`), made by `tools/make_logo_blob.py`.
264	`XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repository root) swaps the logo for a local
265	image at build time. Keep a third-party logo under `vendor/`, out of git.
266	
267	A big blob (Pacman's is 3 MB as C text) is built from `vendor/` by a `pre:`
268	script and never committed; write it to a `.partial` file and rename it.
269	
270	## Pixmap double buffering
271	
272	When: a plain screenhack makes two pixmaps, draws into them and `XCopyArea`s the
273	result to the window (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes, Halftone,
274	Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole). Since #61 this works as copied, but a back
275	buffer costs 434 KB of PSRAM and a full-frame copy each frame, and dirties
276	every row, so the push loses what the dirty rectangle (#52) saves. Draw
277	straight on the canvas instead, as below. (These eight were ported before #61,
278	when the copy from a blank pixmap erased the picture.)
279	
280	- A pinned hash of a blank frame passes silently (`0xa4f79500bd791711ull`, which
281	  is also Pedal's at frame 200). Look at the frame before pinning.
282	- Upstream switches the buffering off under `HAVE_JWXYZ` ("Don't second-guess
283	  Quartz's double-buffering"), or reads a `doubleBuffer` resource. Write
284	  `hacks/<name>_direct.c`: include `screenhack.h` and the math headers, empty
285	  `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`, `#define HAVE_JWXYZ`, include the unmodified hack and
286	  register its `HackEntry`. Exclude the original from `build_src_filter` in all
287	  three environments. `grep HAVE_JWXYZ` first: Interaggregate also uses it for
288	  pixel packing, but only in the 24 and 32 bit cases, and the canvas is 16 bit.
289	- A hack that uses a pixmap as storage needs no wrapper. Truchet draws a canvas
290	  bigger than the window into an 866 by 866 pixmap (1.5 MB of PSRAM) and
291	  scrolls it with `XCopyArea` offsets.
292	
293	## Restart leak test
294	
295	When: the hack restarts itself. Override its cycle resource in the test (for
296	example `*maxCycles: 3`), compare `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()`
297	before and after many restarts, and prove the test sees a leak by removing a
298	`free` in a temporary copy or leaking from a shim function. Never leave the
299	hack changed: `cmp` it afterwards.
300	
301	Measure the growth first, then set the tolerance just above it (Pacman: exactly
302	0, so 512 bytes). A loose one passes a leaked GC; mutation-check by leaking one.
303	
304	On the device, work out how long a restart takes: cycles times the frame time.
305	Substrate's 10,000 cycles at about 160 ms is 27 minutes, and the restart showed
306	at about 25. Capture that long, with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`.
307	
308	## Stopping before the first draw
309	
310	When: the hack allocates on its first `draw` (look for a lazy `initted` flag)
311	but sizes its `free` from values set in `init`. Two quick button presses, or a
312	press with the 90 s rotation, free a hack before it has drawn once. Blaster
313	sets `NUM_ROBOTS` in init, allocates `robots` in draw, and its free loops over
314	`robots[i].lasers`, so freeing it first dereferenced NULL. The dump tool with 0
315	frames exited 139.
316	
317	- `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame` starts and stops every
318	  hack with no frame, so a new port that has this problem fails the host suite.
319	- To fix it without editing the hack, write a wrapper that includes the
320	  unmodified source with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers the hack
321	  itself, with a `free` that makes the loop safe (`hacks/blaster_safe.c`).
322	- A real press is rarely handled in that window: Rod's presses on the device
323	  all landed after the first step. Rely on the test, not on pressing buttons.
324	- An xlockmore hack cannot be re-registered that way: `xlockmore.h` has no
325	  include guard, so the hack's own include redefines `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`
326	  after the wrapper empties it. Swap the callback in the table instead, from a
327	  constructor: `<name>_xlockmore_function_table.hack_init = my_init;`
328	  (`loop_direct.c`, `hypnowheel_single_gl.c`).
329	
330	## Tests that cannot be fooled
331	
332	A test that runs a real hack can pass for the wrong reason. Pyro clears its own
333	window in `init`, so a "starts black" test through Pyro passed with the runner
334	deliberately broken. Test shared runner behaviour with stub hacks
335	(`test_runner_xsft.c`) and mutate the code to see the test fail.
336	
337	A check can also be true before the hack has run. "At least 20 non-black
338	pixels" proved a hack drew, until Substrate started on a white canvas and
339	passed without drawing at all. Compare with the canvas as the hack started, and
340	keep a stub hack that draws nothing, on the colour that fooled the old check, to
341	show the test can fail. When a change alters what every hack starts with (the
342	background colour, an initial canvas), re-read the older tests that assume the
343	old start.
344	
345	A bounds guard can be unreachable through the public API. TinyGL's clipper
346	keeps a line inside the view volume and its viewport maps that to at most pixel
347	63.5, so two of the four guards in the smooth-line plot survived mutation until
348	a test used a viewport bigger than the canvas. Mutate each guard on its own
349	(a scratchpad script that edits, runs the suite and restores in `finally`),
350	and when one survives, find an input that reaches it or say it is defensive.
351	Wrapping bugs can also hide in what is stored, not what is drawn: a depth that
352	wrapped round only showed when a third fill was drawn afterwards.
353	
354	## Background colour
355	
356	The runner paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before `init`,
357	as `screenhack.c` paints the window. Substrate (`.background: white`) depends
358	on it. Every earlier hack asks for black or nothing.
359	
360	## Skipping a hack
361	
362	Threads, GL, Xft and shared memory are not worth porting. Record the name and
363	the reason in `tools/failed_ports.txt` (`name: reason`); the scorer marks it as
364	abandoned.
365	
366	## Worktree setup
367	
368	A fresh worktree lacks the ignored `vendor/`, `.venv/` and `.platformio/`:
369	symlink them from the main checkout. They show as untracked, so `git add`
370	named paths, never `-A`. Adding them to `.git/info/exclude` changes state shared
371	with every worktree: ask Rod first.
372	
373	A worktree session refuses `source`, `$VAR` in a command and `&&` chains with a
374	computed path. Run plain commands with literal paths, for example
375	`PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<worktree>/.platformio ../.venv/bin/pio test -e native`.
376	
377	## Device capture
378	
379	- Pin the hack with `-DSTART_HACK=\"name\"` and add `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`, or the
380	  board rotates to the next hack after 90 s.
381	- Send upload output to a file, never through `head`, and look for "Hash of
382	  data verified".
383	- Capture 150 s or more of serial in the background, longer to see a restart.
384	  Read `step`, `push`, `wait`, heap and PSRAM, and any "Stack canary".
385	- Compare with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: pushes became
386	  41-45 ms on every hack after the byte-order fix, against 31 ms before (#23).
387	- Pinning a frame hash: set the new hack's `kBaseline` entry to `1`, run
388	  `pio test -f test_hacks`, read `Was N` in the failure and convert with
389	  `python3 -c "print('0x%016xull' % N)"`. Pin only after looking at the frame
390	  (and never type the hex by hand: one was wrong).
391	- Showing Rod a hack: flash `-DSTART_HACK=\"first\" -DROTATE_SECONDS=25` with
392	  `XS_LOGO=...` so the new ones come up in order, then tell him which, and that
393	  the button steps backwards (from Pyro it wraps to the last hack).

# Porting assessment

Rough effort to port each xscreensaver hack to the StopWatch X11 shim,
generated from xscreensaver 6.16 by `tools/score_hacks.py`. Regenerate
it with `uv run tools/score_hacks.py`.

## How to read this

- **283 hacks** were scanned: every `hacks/*.c` and `hacks/glx/*.c`
  that registers itself with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`. Another 125
  files (3D models, helper libraries, command-line tools) are excluded and
  listed at the end.
- The scan is static and heuristic. For each 2D hack it counts the Xlib
  calls in the source that the shim does not declare, and it also
  syntax-checks the unmodified source against the shim's headers
  (`cc -fsyntax-only`). Anything the compiler cannot find is a **shim

    uv run tools/wire_hack.py <name> <Class> "<copyright text>" \\

Does the mechanical steps of `.claude/skills/port-hack/adding-a-hack.md`

`firmware/src/hacks/<name>/`, adds the registry entry (last in the button
order), the name to the expected list in `test_hacks.c`, a frame hash of `0`
(skipped until pinned: see "Batches" in that skill), a leak test, and the
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md row. It does not touch `platformio.ini`, write a
wrapper, or fill a shim gap. Read the hack's licence first.

--xlockmore registers with `XLOCKMORE_HACK(name, "Class")`, for a hack built on
xlockmore.h (it has `MI_DISPLAY`); otherwise it expects the hack to define its
own `<name>_hack` through XSCREENSAVER_MODULE.
"""

import argparse
import re
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
UPSTREAM = "vendor/xscreensaver-6.16"


def _insert_before(text: str, marker: str, addition: str) -> str:
    i = text.find(marker)
    if i < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"cannot find `{marker}`")
    return text[:i] + addition + text[i:]


def wire(
    root: Path,
    name: str,
    cls: str,
    copyright_text: str,
    notice: str = "jwz permission notice (above)",
    xlockmore: bool = False,
    glx: bool = False,
) -> None:
    src = root / UPSTREAM / "hacks" / ("glx" if glx else "") / f"{name}.c"
    if not src.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(src)
    dst = root / "firmware" / "src" / "hacks" / name / f"{name}.c"
    registry = root / "firmware" / "src" / "hacks" / "registry.c"
    tests = root / "firmware" / "test" / "test_hacks" / "test_hacks.c"
    notices = root / "THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md"

    reg = registry.read_text()
    if re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(name)}_hack\b", reg):
        raise ValueError(f"{name} is already in registry.c")
    if xlockmore:
        decl = f'XLOCKMORE_HACK({name}, "{cls}");\n'
    else:
        decl = f"extern const HackEntry {name}_hack;\n"
    reg = _insert_before(reg, "const HackEntry *const g_hacks[]", decl + "\n")
    reg, n = re.subn(
        r"    &(\w+)_hack\};", rf"    &\1_hack,\n    &{name}_hack}};", reg, count=1

- Pacman has two build-time patches (`tools/pacman_patch.py`, run by

266	Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.
267	
268	- `unsigned long` is 4 bytes on the device and 8 on the host, so a hack that
269	  allocates arrays of it (Substrate's two 466 by 466 buffers) is twice the size
270	  on the host, and host leak numbers are twice the device's. On the device,
271	  plain `malloc`/`realloc` of about 868 KB reached PSRAM (free PSRAM fell by
272	  1.74 MB) and came back on restart; internal heap barely moved.
273	- The board's `malloc` is `CONFIG_SPIRAM_USE_MALLOC=y` with
274	  `SPIRAM_MALLOC_ALWAYSINTERNAL=4096`: a block up to 4 KB comes from internal
275	  RAM and falls back to PSRAM when that is full, and a bigger one goes to PSRAM
276	  first. An allocation fails only when PSRAM is gone, so a hack's `abort()` on
277	  a failed allocation is not the risk it looks. The cost of a big pattern is
278	  internal heap drained to near zero (Celtic read 1,792 B free) and its data
279	  in slower PSRAM: compare the log's `psram=` with its idle value for the
280	  overflow.
281	- `erase_window` (`erase.c`) follows upstream's contract: the first call draws
282	  nothing and returns a state, so a hack that waits after it (Celtic's 5 s
283	  `*delay2`) waits on the finished picture. The second call starts a one-second
284	  wipe (blinds, circle, fizzle or random lines, picked at random), each later
285	  call draws the next step, and the call after the second is up clears the
286	  window and returns NULL. Progress comes from `double_time()`, not from the
287	  call count, so the wipe lasts a second at any step rate. A test or tool
288	  that does not sleep for a hack's delay must install a clock
289	  (`xshim_set_clock`), or a wipe never ends. Six hacks never call
290	  `eraser_free`, so the display tracks live states and the runner releases
291	  them when a hack stops.
292	- xlockmore hacks (the 40 that include `xlockmore.h`) need `-DSTANDALONE`,
293	  which every PlatformIO env and `score_hacks.py` set; without it they
294	  include `xlock.h` instead. The envs also define `HAVE_MOBILE`, because
295	  otherwise each hack's `XSCREENSAVER_LINK` defines the same global
296	  `xscreensaver_function_table` and two hacks fail to link; the only other
297	  effect is an inert `*ignoreRotation: True` default. Register one in
298	  `hacks/registry.c` with `XLOCKMORE_HACK(<name>, "<Class>")`. The runner runs
299	  the hack's `setup_cb` once and passes `setup_arg` as `init_cb`'s hidden third
300	  argument, as xscreensaver's `screenhack.c` does. Its table is empty until
301	  then. Resources the framework reads but a hack does not define
302	  (`delta3d`, `size`, ...) fall back to `kFrameworkDefaults` in
303	  `x11shim/resources.c`. A `HackEntry`'s `overrides` list beats the hack's own
304	  defaults (Galaxy runs with `count: -3`, at most three galaxies; a count of
305	  -2 or above skips the hack's restart cleanup and leaks); register it with
306	  `XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH`. Galaxy, Drift, Discrete and Flame are built through
307	  `hacks/<name>_single.c`, which includes the framework headers, then
308	  `hacks/single_precision.h` (`double` and the libm calls become `float` and
309	  the `f` versions; the S3's FPU is single-precision only), then the unmodified
310	  hack; the original `.c` is excluded from each env's `build_src_filter`.
311	- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1), arcs and pixmap writes live in
312	  `x11shim/stroke.c`, `arc.c` and `pixmap.c`. Width 0 and 1 keep the old
313	  `canvas_line` path, so hacks that set no wide width are pixel-identical (every
314	  hack's frame is pinned in `test_hacks.c`). Braid is the one registered hack

"""Convert a raw little-endian RGB565 frame dump to PNG (stdlib only).

Run with: uv run tools/rgb565_to_png.py in.raw WIDTH HEIGHT out.png
"""

import struct
import sys
import zlib


def _chunk(kind: bytes, body: bytes) -> bytes:
    crc = zlib.crc32(kind + body) & 0xFFFFFFFF
    return struct.pack(">I", len(body)) + kind + body + struct.pack(">I", crc)


def convert(raw: bytes, w: int, h: int) -> bytes:
    if len(raw) != w * h * 2:
        raise ValueError(f"expected {w * h * 2} bytes for {w}x{h}, got {len(raw)}")
    pixels = struct.unpack(f"<{w * h}H", raw)
    rows = bytearray()
    for y in range(h):
        rows.append(0)
        for p in pixels[y * w : (y + 1) * w]:
            r, g, b = (p >> 11) & 0x1F, (p >> 5) & 0x3F, p & 0x1F
            rows += bytes((r << 3 | r >> 2, g << 2 | g >> 4, b << 3 | b >> 2))
    ihdr = struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", w, h, 8, 2, 0, 0, 0)
    return (
        b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"
        + _chunk(b"IHDR", ihdr)
        + _chunk(b"IDAT", zlib.compress(bytes(rows), 9))
        + _chunk(b"IEND", b"")
    )


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    if len(argv) != 4:
        print(__doc__)
        return 2
    src, w, h, dst = argv[0], int(argv[1]), int(argv[2]), argv[3]
    with open(src, "rb") as f:
        png = convert(f.read(), w, h)
    with open(dst, "wb") as f:
        f.write(png)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1:]))

"""Make every decimal literal in a C file a float, for single-precision builds.

`hacks/single_precision.h` turns the keyword `double` into `float`, but a
literal such as `0.5` is still a double, so `0.5 * x` with a float `x` is done
in double precision, which the ESP32-S3 does in software (Braid's draw loop
called `__muldf3` and `__adddf3` for every coordinate). Giving each literal an
`f` suffix keeps the arithmetic in single precision.

GCC's `-fsingle-precision-constant` does the same, but Apple clang ignores it,
so host tests would run different arithmetic from the board. A source rewrite
gives both the same text.

The copied hack stays byte-identical to upstream. The firmware build writes a
rewritten copy with `firmware/patch_float_literals.py` and compiles that.
"""

import re

_TOKEN = re.compile(
    r"""
      (?P<skip>
          /\*.*?\*/
        | //[^\n]*
        | "(?:\\.|[^"\\\n])*"
        | '(?:\\.|[^'\\\n])*'
      )
    | (?P<literal>
          (?:\d+\.\d+|\.\d+|\d+\.(?![\w.]))(?![\w.])
      )
    """,
    re.VERBOSE | re.DOTALL,
)


def float_literals(source: str) -> str:
    """Appends `f` to each decimal literal outside strings, characters and
    comments. A literal with a suffix or an exponent is left as it is."""
    count = 0

    def replace(match: re.Match[str]) -> str:
        nonlocal count
        if match.group("skip") is not None:
            return match.group(0)
        count += 1
        return match.group(0) + "f"

    out = _TOKEN.sub(replace, source)
    if count == 0:
        raise ValueError("no floating-point literals found; is this the right file?")
    return out

 * The hack blends each anti-aliased hit into its own buffer of pixel values
 * at an alpha of 0.15 times the coverage. In its 16-bit path a hit adds less
 * than one 5-bit step of red or blue, which is dropped, so only green ever
